write.desc: Differentiation of real functions of one variable, from the definition of the derivative and the proofs of the differentiation rules, through Fermat, Rolle and the mean value theorems and what follows from them, to Darboux's theorem, L'Hopital's rule and Taylor's theorem with the Lagrange remainder. These points belong together because each one rests on the derivative as a limit and most of them come from the mean value theorem.

points.name: The derivative as a limit of difference quotients
points.what: Define f'(c) as the limit of (f(x) - f(c))/(x - c) as x tends to c, with c a limit point of the domain, and one-sided derivatives at endpoints. Compute derivatives from the definition (x^n, 1/x, sqrt x) and restate differentiability as f(x) = f(c) + f'(c)(x - c) + r(x), where r(x)/(x - c) tends to 0.
outside: epsilon-delta definition of the limit of a function at a limit point of its domain

points.name: Differentiable implies continuous, but not conversely
points.what: Prove that a function differentiable at c is continuous at c. Show with |x| that the converse fails, and know that continuous functions which are differentiable nowhere exist (Weierstrass), stated without proof.
outside: definition of continuity of a function at a point

points.name: Sum, product and quotient rules
points.what: Prove the derivative rules for f + g, cf, fg and f/g from the definition, using the limit laws and the continuity of a differentiable function, and point out where g(c) != 0 is needed in the quotient rule.
outside: limit laws for limits of functions (sum, product, quotient)

points.name: The chain rule
points.what: Prove (g o f)'(c) = g'(f(c)) f'(c) correctly, avoiding the division by f(x) - f(c) = 0 that breaks the naive proof, for example by writing the difference quotient of g as a function continuous at f(c) (Caratheodory's formulation).
outside: continuity of a composition of continuous functions

points.name: Derivative of an inverse function
points.what: Prove that if f is continuous and strictly monotone on an interval, differentiable at c and f'(c) != 0, then the inverse is differentiable at f(c) with derivative 1/f'(c). Apply this to n-th roots, log and arcsin, and explain why f'(c) = 0 (as for x^3 at 0) breaks differentiability of the inverse.
outside: continuity of the inverse of a continuous strictly monotone function on an interval

points.name: Local extrema and Fermat's theorem
points.what: Define local maxima and minima and prove that at an interior local extremum of a differentiable function the derivative is 0, by comparing the signs of the one-sided difference quotients. Know that the converse fails (x^3) and that endpoints and points of non-differentiability must be checked separately.
outside: limits of functions preserve non-strict inequalities (order limit theorem)

points.name: Rolle's theorem
points.what: Prove that a function continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), with f(a) = f(b), has f'(c) = 0 for some c in (a,b), using the extreme value theorem and Fermat's theorem. Show with examples that each hypothesis is needed.
outside: extreme value theorem for continuous functions on a closed bounded interval

points.name: The mean value theorem
points.what: Prove that f(b) - f(a) = f'(c)(b - a) for some c in (a,b) by applying Rolle's theorem to f minus its chord, read it geometrically as a tangent parallel to the chord, and recognise it as the tool that turns information about f' into information about f.

points.name: Zero derivative and monotonicity from the sign of f'
points.what: Use the mean value theorem to prove that f' = 0 on an interval forces f to be constant, that functions with equal derivatives differ by a constant, and that f' >= 0 (or > 0) gives increasing (or strictly increasing) f. Explain why these fail on domains that are not intervals and why strictly increasing does not imply f' > 0.

points.name: Proving inequalities and Lipschitz bounds with the mean value theorem
points.what: Prove inequalities such as |sin x - sin y| <= |x - y|, log(1 + x) <= x, e^x >= 1 + x and Bernoulli's inequality, and show that a bounded derivative on an interval makes f Lipschitz and therefore uniformly continuous.

points.name: Cauchy's mean value theorem
points.what: Prove that (f(b) - f(a)) g'(c) = (g(b) - g(a)) f'(c) for some c in (a,b) by applying Rolle's theorem to a suitable combination of f and g, and see why applying the ordinary mean value theorem to f and g separately does not give the same c.

points.name: A differentiable function whose derivative is not continuous
points.what: Show that x^2 sin(1/x) (with value 0 at 0) is differentiable everywhere with f'(0) = 0 computed from the definition, while f' has no limit at 0, and contrast it with x sin(1/x), which is continuous but not differentiable at 0. Know the terms C^1 and continuously differentiable.
outside: squeeze theorem for limits of functions

points.name: Darboux's theorem
points.what: Prove that a derivative has the intermediate value property on an interval even when it is not continuous, using the extreme value theorem and Fermat's theorem, and conclude that a derivative cannot have a jump discontinuity (so, for example, the sign function is not a derivative).
outside: extreme value theorem for continuous functions on a closed bounded interval

points.name: L'Hopital's rule: the 0/0 form
points.what: Prove that if f and g tend to 0 at a and f'/g' tends to L, then f/g tends to L, using Cauchy's mean value theorem, state the hypotheses precisely (including g' != 0 near a), and give an example where the limit of f/g exists but the limit of f'/g' does not.

points.name: L'Hopital's rule: the infinity/infinity form and limits at infinity
points.what: Prove the version where |g| tends to infinity, which needs a more careful epsilon argument, and extend both forms to limits as x tends to plus or minus infinity, for example to compare the growth of log x, x^n and e^x.
outside: limits at infinity and infinite limits of functions

points.name: Higher derivatives and the classes C^n
points.what: Define f'', f^(n), the classes C^n and C^infinity on an interval, and see that each class is strictly smaller than the one before (x^n|x|-type and x^2 sin(1/x)-type examples). Know the Leibniz rule for the n-th derivative of a product as a stated formula.

points.name: Taylor polynomials
points.what: Define the Taylor polynomial of degree n of f at a as the unique polynomial of degree at most n whose derivatives up to order n match those of f at a, and compute standard ones (e^x, sin x, cos x, log(1 + x), (1 + x)^r).

points.name: Taylor's theorem with the Lagrange remainder
points.what: Prove that if f^(n+1) exists on an interval then f(x) = P_n(x) + f^(n+1)(c)(x - a)^(n+1)/(n+1)! for some c between a and x, by applying Rolle's theorem (or Cauchy's mean value theorem) repeatedly to a suitable auxiliary function, and see the mean value theorem as the case n = 0.

points.name: Estimating errors with Taylor's theorem
points.what: Use the Lagrange remainder to bound the error of a Taylor approximation, choose n to reach a given accuracy (for example e or sin(0.1) to six decimals), and prove inequalities such as 1 - x^2/2 <= cos x.
outside: standard sequence limits such as x^n/n! tending to 0

points.name: The second derivative test for local extrema
points.what: Prove that f'(c) = 0 and f''(c) > 0 (or < 0) give a strict local minimum (or maximum), explain why the test is silent when f''(c) = 0, and state the higher-order test using the first nonzero derivative.

points.name: Convex functions
points.what: Define convexity by the chord inequality, show it is equivalent to increasing slopes of chords, and prove that for differentiable f convexity means f' is increasing (and f'' >= 0 when f is twice differentiable) and that the graph lies above its tangent lines. Use this briefly to prove inequalities such as the AM-GM inequality via log.

where.title: Stephen Abbott, Understanding Analysis (2nd ed.)
where.detail: Chapter 5, The Derivative (5.2 derivatives and the intermediate value property, 5.3 mean value theorems and L'Hospital's rule, 5.4 a continuous nowhere-differentiable function); Taylor's theorem with the Lagrange remainder in Section 6.6

where.title: Robert G. Bartle and Donald R. Sherbert, Introduction to Real Analysis
where.detail: Chapter 6, Differentiation: 6.1 The derivative, 6.2 The mean value theorem, 6.3 L'Hospital's rules, 6.4 Taylor's theorem (including convex functions)

where.title: Michael Spivak, Calculus
where.detail: Chapters 9 to 12 (derivatives, differentiation rules, significance of the derivative, with an appendix on convexity, inverse functions) and Chapter 20, Approximation by polynomial functions

where.title: Walter Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis (3rd ed.)
where.detail: Chapter 5, Differentiation (mean value theorems, Darboux's theorem, L'Hospital's rule, Taylor's theorem)
